This could include changing the timing, sequence and amount of transactions; creating false paper trails or altering existing records; or using un-traceable money sources such as cash and intermediary banks. Another common tactic is to inappropriately reallocate income among different accounts, hiding illegitimate sums in costly research and development projects or off-balance sheet entities. Additionally, some fraudsters will create 'shell' corporations that appear legitimate but never produce products or services, while instead taking funds out of the company under false pretences. Lastly it may also be beneficial to create fictitious suppliers so payments appear valid but are ultimately transferred through personal bank accounts belonging to those involved in fraudulent activities; these practices enable individuals with access levels at a company level to divert fund from any specific account within their entity which goes undetected until further investigated/noticed during period end checks .  These strategies can prove successful if not fully explored for a prolonged period of time as detecting and tracing each transaction becomes even more difficult. Regular reviews together with experienced financial analysts who are well conversant on recognizing potential trends can help uncover irregularities before too much damage has been done
